name: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom
info: A Hellenistic Greek kingdom in Central Asia founded by the Seleucid satrap Diodotus I, remembered for its cities such as Ai-Khanoum, its coinage and its spread of Greek culture towards India and China.

facts.capital: Bactra (also called Zariaspa); Heliocles later moved his seat to the Kabul valley
facts.founder: Diodotus I Soter, Seleucid satrap of Bactria
facts.successor: The Yuezhi, later the Kushan Empire; in the south the Indo-Greek Kingdom

t: Diodotus, satrap of Bactria, seceded from the Seleucid Empire around the middle of the 3rd century BC; the exact date is unsettled, between a high chronology of c. 255 BC and a low one of c. 246 BC.
Under Demetrius, son of Euthydemus, the Bactrian Greeks invaded north-western India between 190 and 180 BC, creating the Indo-Greek Kingdom.
The Bactrian language continued to be written in the Greek script until the 9th century AD, nearly a thousand years after the kingdom fell.
dyk: The Greco-Bactrians were the first in the world to issue coins of cupro-nickel, an alloy at the time known only to the Chinese; copper-nickel was not used again in coinage until the 19th century.
ev: Diodotus, Seleucid satrap of Bactria, secedes and becomes king; the date is disputed between c. 255 and c. 246 BC
Euthydemus overthrows the dynasty of Diodotus II and founds his own
The Seleucid king Antiochus III attacks Euthydemus, who resists a three-year siege in Bactra
Antiochus III recognises Euthydemus and offers a daughter to his son Demetrius
Demetrius invades north-western India, founding the Indo-Greek Kingdom
Eucratides seizes power in a coup and founds the Eucratid dynasty
Eucratides is killed by his own son; Ai-Khanoum is burnt during nomadic invasions
The Yuezhi expand into Bactria and Heliocles moves his capital to the Kabul valley

sections.foundation:
Greeks lived in Bactria long before the kingdom. Under Darius I most of the people of Barca in Cyrenaica were deported there, and under Xerxes I the descendants of Greek priests from near Didyma were forcibly relocated to the region. Alexander the Great crossed the Hindu Kush in 329 BCE and conquered Bactria, placing garrisons at Bactra, Maracanda and Cyropolis and settling Greek mercenaries in new colonies along the Oxus and the Jaxartes; he also massacred the Greek community settled there before him. After Alexander's death Bactria passed to his general Seleucus I Nicator.

Diodotus, the Seleucid satrap of Bactria, seceded and became king Diodotus I. The ancient sources conflict: a high chronology puts his secession about 255 BC, a low one in the mid-240s BC, connecting it with the Third Syrian War. Justin calls him the governor of the thousand cities of Bactria. When Arsaces founded the Parthian state, Bactria was cut off from the Greek world. Diodotus II, his son, allied with Arsaces against Seleucus II.
sections.socioeconomy:
The kingdom was highly urbanised and, to Justin, one of the richest of the East, the extremely prosperous empire of the thousand cities. Only a few of its cities have been excavated, among them Ai-Khanoum and Bactra (modern Balkh). Ai-Khanoum had a Greek theatre, a gymnasium and houses with colonnaded courtyards, Corinthian columns and fragments of a statue 5–6 metres tall; it was burnt around 145 BC and never resettled. Takht-i Sangin in Tajikistan held a large temple to the Oxus. Other cities include Alexandria Eschate, Eucratideia and an Amphipolis named after the Macedonian city.

Military colonists held allotments of land called kleros, and once the Parthians cut the overland routes, sea trade with Greek Egypt developed. Around 126 BC the Han envoy Zhang Qian found a population of 1,000,000 or more, people who farmed, lived in cities and were clever at commerce, with a great market at the capital, Lanshi (Bactra), where he saw bamboo from Qiong and cloth from Shu bought in India. His report led the Han to send envoys to Central Asia and to the development of the Silk Road.
sections.military:
Bactrian cavalry had long been famous: 9,000 Bactrian horsemen fought for Darius at the Battle of Gaugamela, and Alexander added Bactrians to his companion cavalry. Greek garrisons were housed in fortresses called phrouria and in the major cities, and military colonists numbering in the tens of thousands were trained as a Macedonian army. The kingdom's army was multi-ethnic: Greek colonists formed pike phalanxes, supported by local Bactrian light infantry and mercenary thureophoroi; a very large cavalry of Bactrian, Sogdian and other horsemen, cataphracts and small elite companion units; and Indian war elephants, shown on coins with towers for archers.

Around 210 BC Antiochus III attacked Euthydemus, who commanded 10,000 horsemen, lost a battle on the Arius and then held Bactra through a three-year siege until Antiochus recognised him. Demetrius completed the invasion of north-western India by 175 BC. Eucratides is said to have broken a siege by Demetrius, king of the Indians, who came with 60,000 men, but he was later repulsed by Menander I and defeated by the Parthian king Mithridates I.
sections.governance:
The kingdom was ruled by three Greek dynasties. The first dynasty began with the satrap Diodotus I, who took the title of basileus, and his son Diodotus II. Euthydemus, an Ionian Greek from Magnesia according to Polybius and possibly satrap of Sogdiana, overthrew Diodotus II around 230–220 BC; his rule reached into Sogdiana and Ferghana beyond Alexandria Eschate. An inscription from the Kulob area, dated 200–195 BC, calls Euthydemus the greatest of all kings and his son Demetrius I Demetrios Kallinikos, the Glorious Conqueror.

Eucratides I, either a general of Demetrius or an ally of the Seleucids, overthrew the Euthydemids around 170 BC, probably dethroning Antimachus I and Antimachus II. Several kings often ruled at once in different regions, which are not well known. Eucratides struck coins at many Indian mints, possibly as far as the Jhelum, and associated a son with his rule. The kings displayed themselves on coins with individual portraits and distinct headgear, such as the kausia, and from Pantaleon onward issued bilingual coins of the Indian standard.
sections.impact:
The Greco-Bactrians kept contact with the Mediterranean and with India, with which they exchanged ambassadors. Ai-Khanoum may have been one of the primary channels of Western artistic influence into India, in the Pillars of Ashoka and the Pataliputra capital. Agathocles (ruled 190–180 BC) issued square coins bearing the first known representations of Indian deities; six were found at Ai-Khanoum in 1970. Their successors in India, the Indo-Greeks, spread Greek art that led to the Greco-Buddhist art of Gandhara.

From Alexandria Eschate the Greco-Bactrians may have led expeditions as far as Kashgar and Ürümqi, the first known contacts between China and the West around 220 BC, and Strabo wrote that they extended their empire as far as the Seres. Their coins rank among the finest Greek numismatic art, including the largest gold coin of the Hellenistic world, minted by Eucratides. The Yuezhi who followed them adopted the Greek alphabet for their language and Greek gods for their pantheon, and the Bactrian language was written in Greek script until the 9th century AD.
sections.decline:
Eucratides was killed around 145 BC by his son and joint king, either Eucratides II or Heliocles I, who by Justin's account drove his chariot over his father's body. Mithridates I of Parthia took the satrapies west of the Arius, Tapuria and Traxiane, and in 141 BC the Greco-Bactrians joined the Seleucid Demetrius II against Parthia, without lasting success. Heliocles I ruled what remained, weakened and open to nomadic invasion.

Pushed west by the Xiongnu and the Wusun, the Yuezhi reached the land north of the Oxus, and around 140 BC the Saka began to invade Parthia and Bactria. When Zhang Qian visited around 126 BC he found the Yuezhi holding Bactria under their sway and the country without a great ruler, only petty chiefs ruling its cities. Around 120 BC the Yuezhi expanded into Bactria, and Heliocles abandoned it for the Kabul valley, making him technically the last Greco-Bactrian king. Greek populations persisted, and the Indo-Greek kings ruled south of the Hindu Kush until around AD 10. The Yuezhi later founded the Kushan Empire.

summary: The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom was a Hellenistic Greek state in Central Asia, founded when the satrap Diodotus I broke from the Seleucids in the mid-3rd century BC. Under the Euthydemid and Eucratid dynasties it ruled Bactria and Sogdiana, invaded India and struck celebrated coins, until Parthian defeats and the Yuezhi ended it around 120 BC.

Tarn, W. W., The Greeks in Bactria and India (Cambridge University Press, 1966)

pointDescs.-256: Diodotus I secedes from the Seleucid Empire and becomes king, by the high chronology.
pointDescs.-247: The Ptolemies capture Antioch; the rise of Parthia cuts Bactria off from the Greek world.
pointDescs.-230: Euthydemus overthrows Diodotus II and extends his rule into Sogdiana and Ferghana.
pointDescs.-210: Antiochus III attacks Euthydemus, who loses a battle on the Arius and is besieged in Bactra.
pointDescs.-206: Antiochus III recognises Euthydemus after a three-year siege and offers a daughter to Demetrius.
pointDescs.-200: An inscription of 200–195 BC calls Euthydemus the greatest of all kings; the kingdom expands west.
pointDescs.-180: Demetrius's invasion of north-western India founds the Indo-Greek Kingdom.
pointDescs.-171: Eucratides seizes power and campaigns in India; the kingdom reaches its peak.
pointDescs.-145: Eucratides is killed by his son, and Ai-Khanoum is burnt during nomadic invasions.
pointDescs.-141: The Greco-Bactrians ally with the Seleucid Demetrius II against Parthia after losing territory to Mithridates I.
pointDescs.-132: The Yuezhi, driven from the Ili valley by the Wusun, move towards the land north of the Oxus.
pointDescs.-126: Zhang Qian finds Bactria under Yuezhi sway, ruled by petty chiefs.
pointDescs.-120: The Yuezhi expand into Bactria and Heliocles moves his capital to the Kabul valley.

notes: The founding date is disputed: the lead says about 256 BC, the history section around 250 BC with a high (c. 255) and low (c. 246) chronology; the first event and point follow the register's -256 with the hedge.
The lead says the kingdom may have reached the borders of the Qin State by about 230 BC; left out as speculative.
The article dates the Arius battle variously 210 and 208 BC; 'around 210 BC' is used.
